name: MEH BELLA Anderson
missingPieces: D1 omits two of the ten findings entirely: stored XSS in comments (A03/CWE-79, capture 02:18:47 cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443) and path traversal (A01/CWE-22, capture 02:24:02 files/?path=/etc/passwd -> root:x:0:0:). D2 chain is only four hops and skips stored XSS (02:18:47), open redirect (02:21:13) and the path-traversal file read (02:24:02).
feedback: D1 is a strong but incomplete catalogue. You nailed the core five with quoted source lines: SQL injection (A03/CWE-89, lines 61-63), unsalted MD5 (CWE-328 is a fine variant of CWE-916, line 63), JWT alg:none (Token 2 header), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (line 30), and the missing exp claim (CWE-613, Token 3). XXE (line 18) and the cookie Secure-flag gap (line 79) and the open redirect (lines 82-83) are all there with evidence, and your decoy call is correct: the b64url helpers are the safe construct and you proved it at the mechanism level rather than inventing an exploit, which is exactly right. What costs you is two whole missing findings, the stored XSS at 02:18:47 with the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 and the path traversal at 02:24:02 hitting /etc/passwd, so this is an eight-of-ten catalogue, not a full one. Your decoy proof would have been airtight if you had named hash_equals() as the constant-time branch that makes HS256 verification sound. D2 is where the report thins out. Your chain reconciles SQLi at 02:15:31, the 312-row bulk pull at 02:16:04, and XXE, but it stops at four hops and never threads the stored XSS, the open redirect, or the file-read hop, so the kill chain reads incomplete. Your CVSS table lists nine vectors, which is good coverage, but only the SQLi entry carries a justifying sentence and the rest are bare scores, which is half credit per the rubric; also your SQLi vector reads S:C/A:N at 10.0 when the bypass does not change scope and does not touch availability, so the defensible value is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. Your impact paragraph does state the 312 customers, the BoltCash six-week window, and an explicit assumption that the CSV holds live production records, which is the right instinct, but the headline figure of 2,145,500,120.50 NGN is off by roughly two orders of magnitude: the balances top out near 950k NGN each and sum to tens of millions, not billions, so re-derive that from the actual export rather than carrying the inflated total into every deliverable. D3 is your best work. The executive summary is readable and lands on a customers-and-naira headline, the threat model correctly flags that the forged admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, your findings are each tied to a file and line, your decoy statement is correct, and your earliest-break reasoning (kill the alg:none acceptance to sever the chain at Hop 2) is sound. Critically you ordered remediation by risk-reduction efficiency with explicit effort hours rather than by CVSS severity, and your two detection stopgaps each name an exact field and a false-positive rate, so those rows score full. The only drag is the same inflated naira figure and the two missing findings flowing through. D4 answers all four prompts, cites ISC2 Canon II and IV by number in a load-bearing way, names NDPA 2023 Section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC duty tied to the 312 customers, and anchors to your own findings, which is solid; it would be stronger with Section 41 (notifying data subjects on high risk) and a little more length in your own voice. I looked for room to round up and your D3 and D4 already carry you, so no inflation was needed. The single most important fix: complete the catalogue and the chain, the stored XSS at 02:18:47 and the path traversal at 02:24:02 are live hops you left on the table, and correct the naira impact to the real tens-of-millions figure.
